notes.meaning: Balaam asks King Balak to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams for sacrifice. Pagan peoples often used the number seven in rituals to try to win the favor of the gods. Balaam thought this elaborate ceremony would please the God of Israel and make Him allow a curse.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The seven altars and multiple animal sacrifices reflect pagan divination customs, where large numbers of animals provided organs like livers for seers to inspect.

notes.meaning: Balak quickly obeys Balaam's orders, and together they sacrifice a bull and a ram on each altar. In ancient times, pagan kings often acted as priests during important state ceremonies. Balak spared no expense because he desperately wanted to defeat Israel.

Balaam tells the king to wait beside the offerings while he goes alone to a bare hill. In the ancient world, diviners went to high, solitary places to look for signs in nature, such as the flight of birds. Balaam hoped the Lord might appear to him there and give him a sign.

God meets Balaam on the hill, even though Balaam was a corrupt diviner using pagan methods. Balaam immediately boasts of the seven altars and sacrifices he prepared, as if God owed him a favor in return. But God cannot be bribed by outward religious acts.

The Lord places a specific message directly into Balaam's mouth and tells him to go back to Balak. Just as God previously made Balaam's donkey speak, He now takes control of Balaam's own voice. God alone decides what message will be delivered.

Balaam returns and finds Balak still waiting by the sacrifices with the Moabite leaders. The king was eagerly waiting to hear a curse against Israel. Everyone present expected the famous seer to deliver the ruin of their enemies.

Balaam begins speaking his inspired message in elevated, poetic language. He reminds Balak that he was summoned all the way from the eastern mountains of Aram to curse and denounce the people of Jacob. Balak hired him to declare God's anger against Israel, but the prophet cannot speak on his own authority.

Balaam admits that he is completely powerless to curse a people whom God has not cursed. No magic spell or human wishing can change what the Lord has decided. Since God has chosen to bless Israel, any attempt to harm them through sorcery will fail.

Looking down from the rocky heights, Balaam sees Israel spread out across the plain. He sees that they are a people set apart by God, entirely distinct from all other nations in their laws, worship, and divine protection. God's people are called to live holy lives, separated from the ungodly ways of the world around them.

Balaam marvels at Israel's vast numbers, which fulfill God's ancient promise to make Abraham's family as countless as the dust. Seeing their special favor with God, Balaam wishes that he could share the peaceful and blessed end of the righteous. Yet desiring a godly death means nothing if a person is unwilling to live a godly life.

King Balak reacts with shock and fury when he hears Balaam bless Israel instead of cursing them. He had paid for a curse to ruin his enemies, but Balaam gave them only honor and favor. God turned the king's wicked plan into utter frustration.

Balaam defends himself by explaining that he is forced to speak only what the Lord puts in his mouth. Even though he wanted the king's reward, he could not override God's absolute control. God shows that human voices must ultimately submit to His will.

Balak refuses to give up and asks Balaam to try again from a different viewpoint. He thinks the huge size of the camp might have frightened Balaam, so he takes him to a place where only the edge of the camp is visible. Superstitious people often imagine that changing locations or angles will change spiritual outcomes.

Balak brings Balaam to a lookout on Mount Pisgah and sets up another seven altars, offering a bull and a ram on each. The king repeats the expensive sacrifices in hopes of convincing God to change His mind. His tireless effort shows how far the enemies of God will go to oppose His people.

Balaam instructs Balak to remain by the burning sacrifices while he steps aside to consult God once more. He seeks private communion to hear what the Lord will reveal. Even in his corrupt state, Balaam knew that any real answer must come from God alone.

The Lord meets with Balaam again and gives him another message to deliver to the king. God does not allow His word to be altered, but uses this second meeting to confirm His first blessing. Balaam is commanded to return and report exactly what God revealed.

Balaam comes back and finds Balak and the Moabite princes still standing beside the offerings. Anxious to hear the result, Balak asks what the Lord has spoken, still hoping for good news. The king wanted God to serve his agenda, but God speaks only the truth.

Balaam commands Balak to stand up and listen carefully to the solemn oracle from God. The formal call to attention shows that the message carries divine authority that even an earthly king must respect. Balak is called by name to hear what the God of Israel has decided.

God is not like fickle human beings who lie, break promises, or change their minds because of unexpected problems. Everything the Lord promises, He has both the will and the power to accomplish. Because God never changes His eternal purposes, His commitment to bless His people cannot be broken.

Balaam explains that he received an absolute command from God to bless Israel. Because God Himself pronounced the blessing, Balaam has no power to cancel or reverse it. The fate of nations rests solely on God's decree, not on the desires of men.

God looks upon Israel as His chosen covenant people and sees no unfaithfulness or rebellion that would cause Him to abandon them to ruin. The Lord is present among them as their King, and His people shout with joy and confidence in His victory. As long as they remain under God's protection, no outside power can conquer them.

God is the One who brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt and continues to guide them with invincible strength. Their power is compared to the mighty horns of a wild ox, an animal known for its fierce, untamable energy. Israel is no longer a weak band of slaves, but a mighty nation backed by the Almighty.

No magic spell, omen, or sorcery has any power to harm God's protected people. Instead of falling before dark powers, Israel will see God perform such great miracles that people will say, 'Look at what God has done!' Believers who trust in the Lord are completely safe from every occult force.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the line as 'there is no divination in Israel,' meaning Israel does not practice sorcery because God speaks to them directly through prophets.

notes.meaning: Balaam compares Israel to a fierce lion rising up to hunt and conquer its prey. The nation will not rest until it wins total victory over its enemies in the land of Canaan. Instead of Moab crushing Israel, Balak now learns that his own kingdom is in grave danger from this unstoppable army.

In complete frustration, Balak begs Balaam to say nothing at all rather than bless Israel again. If the prophet cannot curse the Israelites to weaken them, the king at least wants him to stop building up their morale. Balak's schemes are crumbling, leaving him desperate to silence God's word.

Balaam reminds Balak that he had warned him from the very beginning: he can do only what the Lord commands. He cannot alter God's truth to please a king or gain a reward. Even a sinful prophet was forced to admit that God's sovereign will cannot be bought or silenced.

Balak refuses to give up and asks Balaam to come to yet another location. He hopes that God might look more favorably on a curse from this new spot. Superstitious minds often believe that persistence or changing outward settings can bend God's will to their own desires.

Balak leads Balaam to the summit of Mount Peor, a mountain overlooking the barren desert and the camp of Israel below. This high place was a center of pagan worship dedicated to the idol Baal-peor. Balak hoped this idol's territory might help him gain an advantage against Israel's God.

For the third time, Balaam orders Balak to build seven altars and bring seven bulls and seven rams for sacrifice. Even after God had twice refused to curse Israel, the men repeat the same ritual. They still clung to the vain hope that enough animal blood might change God's mind.

Balak follows Balaam's instructions once again, sacrificing a bull and a ram on each of the seven altars. The king was willing to pay any cost and spend any amount of time to destroy Israel. But human schemes and expensive rituals are powerless against the unchanging promises of God.
